title: How Many People Actually Achieve the Life They Planned at 22?
metaTitle: How Many People Achieve the Life They Planned at 22?
metaDescription: Almost no one's life follows their 22-year-old plan, and the research explains why. Milestones shifted later, and the self that made the plan won't last.
keyFinding: Almost no one's life follows the plan they made at 22, and the research suggests this is the norm rather than a failure — the self that made the plan predictably changes, and life's milestones have shifted later and grown more variable.
honestAnswer: Very few people end up living the specific life they planned at 22 — and the research suggests that diverging from that plan is statistically normal, not a sign of failure. Part of the reason is built into how minds work: the person who made the plan is not the person who has to live it, because your values, preferences, and personality keep changing in ways you reliably underestimate. The other part is structural: the milestones that 22-year-old plans are built around now happen later and follow far less predictable paths than the script assumes.
whatDataShows: A key finding is the 'End of History Illusion,' from Quoidbach, Gilbert, and Wilson (2013) in Science. Across a large sample, people of every age acknowledged they had changed a great deal in the past decade — but consistently predicted they would change very little in the next one. In other words, we tend to feel that who we are now is roughly who we'll always be. That illusion is strongest when we're young, which means a plan made at 22 is built on the assumption that the 22-year-old's values and goals will last — an assumption the data says is usually wrong.

Meanwhile, the milestones those plans assume have moved. The US median age at first marriage has risen into roughly the late twenties to around 30 (US Census Bureau), first births have shifted later, and homeownership tends to come later than it did for previous generations. Careers have grown less linear: median job tenure is on the order of four years (US Bureau of Labor Statistics), so the steady single-track career many plans assume is no longer the default.

Layered on top is affective forecasting — our well-documented tendency to mispredict how future outcomes will make us feel. We overestimate how much achieving a given goal will satisfy us and for how long. So even the parts of a 22-year-old plan that do come true often don't land the way they were imagined to. Between a changing self, shifting milestones, and forecasting errors, divergence from the plan isn't the exception. It's close to the rule.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels like a personal shortfall because the plan was specific and vivid, while the reasons it didn't pan out are diffuse and invisible. You remember exactly what you pictured — the role, the timeline, the city — but you don't see the slow drift of your own values, or the way the whole population's milestones quietly moved later. So the gap reads as 'I fell short of my plan' rather than 'the plan was built on a self and a schedule that no longer exist.'

The End of History Illusion makes this especially sharp. Because we feel like our current self is our permanent self, we extend the same feeling backward and assume the 22-year-old who made the plan should still be authoritative. But that person was, in a real sense, someone else — with different information, different priorities, and a different idea of what mattered. Holding your present life to their plan is comparing yourself to a stranger's wishes.

Comparison amplifies it again. The people who appear to be 'on track' are usually visible only at their milestones, not in the detours and revised plans behind them. And the cultural script that says certain things should happen by certain ages was written for an era when those milestones genuinely did happen earlier — so measuring yourself against it means measuring against a timetable that no longer describes the people around you.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most useful reframe the research supports is to hold plans loosely. If your values and preferences will predictably keep changing — and the End of History Illusion says you'll underestimate exactly that — then treating a 22-year-old plan as binding optimizes for a person who no longer exists. Periodically updating what you're aiming for, in light of who you've actually become, fits the evidence far better than grimly executing an outdated blueprint.

Because affective forecasting is unreliable, the research suggests weighting actual present-day experience over predicted future satisfaction. Rather than chasing a goal because your younger self assumed it would feel a certain way, it's more reliable to notice what genuinely engages and satisfies you now, and to let that information revise the plan. Small experiments tend to teach you more about what fits than confident long-range prediction does.

It also helps to replace the cultural timetable with the real distribution. Knowing that first marriage now commonly lands in the late twenties or around 30, that homeownership and first births come later, and that median job tenure is only about four years, reframes 'I'm off-plan' as 'I'm roughly where the data says people now are.' Anchoring to actual population timing tends to dissolve a lot of the felt failure.
whatDoesNotHelp: Rigidly executing the 22-year-old plan as if changing course were failure tends to backfire, because it locks you into goals chosen by a self with different values and worse information. The End of History Illusion makes this trap feel virtuous — like loyalty to your 'real' self — when it's often loyalty to a self you've already outgrown.

Measuring yourself against the old cultural timetable doesn't help and produces a false sense of being behind. The script's milestone ages were drawn from an era when people did marry, buy homes, and settle into careers earlier; holding yourself to those ages compares your real life to a schedule the current data no longer supports.

Doubling down on a goal purely because you once predicted it would make you happy is its own pitfall, given how unreliable affective forecasting is. Pursuing something because the 22-year-old assumed it would feel a certain way — rather than because it actually engages you now — is exactly the kind of prediction the research warns tends to miss.
realNumbersInContext: The structural shift in milestones is the clearest number to anchor to. The US median age at first marriage is now in the range of the late twenties to around 30 (US Census Bureau), up substantially over recent decades, with first births and homeownership similarly later. Median job tenure of roughly four years (US Bureau of Labor Statistics) means the typical worker changes jobs many times, so a single-track career — the backbone of many 22-year-old plans — is now the exception rather than the assumption.

The psychological numbers reinforce it. In Quoidbach, Gilbert, and Wilson's 2013 study, people across the age range underestimated their future change even though they could clearly see how much they'd already changed — an effect found consistently across a large sample. The precise size of anyone's future change can't be predicted, but the direction of the error is robust: we expect to stay the same and don't. Put together, a plan made at 22 is built on a self that will shift and a timetable that already has.
keyTakeaways: Almost no one ends up living the specific life they planned at 22 — diverging from it is statistically normal, not failure.
The self that made the plan keeps changing in ways it underestimates (the End of History Illusion), strongest when young.
The milestones plans assume have moved: first marriage now lands in the late twenties to around 30, and first births and homeownership come later.
Careers are less linear — median job tenure is about four years, so a single-track career is now the exception.
Affective forecasting is unreliable, so even the parts of a plan that come true often don't land the way they were imagined.

examples.body: Because the End of History Illusion makes your current self feel permanent, you assume the 22-year-old who made the plan should still be authoritative. But that person had different information, different priorities, and a different idea of what mattered. Holding your present life to their plan is, in a real sense, comparing yourself to a stranger's wishes.

examples.title: 'Off-plan' at 30
examples.body: Someone at 30 feels behind their 22-year-old blueprint — not married, renting, already on a third job. Measured against the actual distribution, that is close to typical: first marriage now commonly lands in the late twenties to around 30, homeownership and first births come later, and median job tenure is only about four years. Being 'off-plan' usually just means being roughly where the data says people now are.

faqs.question: Is it normal that my life looks nothing like I planned at 22?
faqs.answer: Yes — it's close to the norm. Almost no one's life follows their early-twenties plan, both because the self that made the plan keeps changing in ways we underestimate (the End of History Illusion) and because life's milestones now happen later and far less predictably than the old script assumed.

faqs.question: Why do plans made when we're young so rarely work out?
faqs.answer: Three reasons the research points to: our values and personalities keep changing (and we underestimate that change), the milestones plans assume — marriage, homeownership, a linear career — have shifted later and grown more variable, and we systematically mispredict how future outcomes will actually feel (affective forecasting errors).

faqs.question: What is the End of History Illusion?
faqs.answer: It's the finding (Quoidbach, Gilbert, and Wilson, 2013) that people readily acknowledge how much they've changed over the past decade but consistently underestimate how much they'll change in the next one. We tend to feel our current self is permanent — so plans built on it are built on a self that won't last.

faqs.question: Does this mean planning is pointless?
faqs.answer: No — it means planning should be loose and revisable rather than binding. Plans are useful as direction, but treating a 22-year-old's specific blueprint as fixed optimizes for a person who no longer exists. Updating goals as you learn who you've become fits the evidence better than rigidly executing the original.

faqs.question: How do I stop feeling like I'm behind my old plan?
faqs.answer: Replace the old cultural timetable with the real distribution: first marriage now commonly lands in the late twenties to around 30, homeownership and first births come later, and median job tenure is only about four years. Measured against where people actually are now, being 'off-plan' usually just means being normal.
